text: A single script is fine until there's more than one step, the steps depend on each other in order, one needs to run on a schedule, and something needs to happen when a step fails at 3 AM with nobody watching. Orchestration is defining tasks, their order, their schedule, and failure handling as a first-class, inspectable thing.

Airflow is an open-source orchestration platform — you define pipelines as Python code called a DAG, and Airflow handles scheduling, tracking every run, retrying failures, and giving you a real UI. This course sits right after dbt and Snowflake for a reason: dbt models the data, Snowflake stores it, Airflow triggers the whole pipeline on a schedule, reliably.

Everything happens inside Airflow's own purpose-built web UI. Every cell in that run-history grid is one task, one run — green succeeded, red failed, orange is running. Nothing here is inferred, it's the actual execution history.

This is the biggest practical difference from a cron job with no visibility: when something fails, you don't SSH into a server and grep a log file — you look at this screen and know immediately which task, which run, and with one more click, why.
Next lesson: the DAG concept — what a Directed Acyclic Graph actually is, and why that specific structure is what makes all of this possible.
